title: Introducing Kiro Crew: AWS's Open-Source AI Agent Orchestrator
excerpt: AWS open-sourced a persistent workspace that coordinates AI coding agents across sessions, schedules, and repos. Here's what it actually does and why it matters.
content_html:
It's Friday afternoon. You're wrapping up. A teammate pings about a latency spike and needs your help investigating. You know the drill: pull up CloudWatch, cross-reference three repos, check the last time this happened, run diagnostic queries. None of it is hard. All of it requires you to be the glue between six different tools.

What if you could message your AI agents, say "find what we did last time, write it up, send it to the team," and head out?

That's Kiro Crew. And it launched on August 4, 2026.

What Kiro Crew actually is

Kiro Crew is an open-source (Apache 2.0), persistent development workspace. An orchestration layer that coordinates multiple AI agents, preserves context across sessions, schedules recurring work, and keeps running while you're offline.

The origin story matters. Three engineers inside Amazon built a side project called MeshClaw. They wanted something simple: kick off a task, walk away, come back to something reviewable. Run several tasks at once instead of babysitting one prompt at a time.

Then other Amazon builders picked it up. Not because someone mandated it. Because engineers kept hitting gaps in their workflows, fixing them, and pushing the fix upstream. In less than six months, 39,000+ Amazon builders adopted it. Nearly 500 contributors shipped 597 updates at an average pace of 143 weekly commits.

That organic adoption is the strongest signal. The fact that thousands of engineers chose to use it and hundreds chose to improve it tells you more than any feature list.

The problem it solves (and why I care)

After 10+ years of building cloud infrastructure across client engagements, I've accepted a frustrating truth: I spend more time being the "glue" between tools than doing actual engineering work.

The Kiro Crew blog post nails this. Developers are the integration layer between their own tools.

I feel this every single day. I have Kiro CLI open, CloudWatch in one tab, GitHub in another, a Slack thread I need to follow up on, three PRs waiting for review, and a deployment that broke overnight. The moment I step away, everything stalls. Nobody reconnects the context. Nobody pushes the migration forward. Nobody notices the flaky test reappeared.

I've been using Kiro CLI for months now. It's good inside a single session. You prompt, it responds, it does solid work. But close the tab? Next time you open it, the context is gone. You spend the first ten minutes re-explaining what you're working on. Your steering files carry over, but the working memory of "where were we?" doesn't.

Kiro Crew breaks that pattern by making the workspace persistent. Memory carries forward. Corrections become lasting lessons. Repeated patterns become reusable skills. And work continues on a schedule even when you're not at your keyboard.

As an AWS Community Builder who's been writing about Kiro since its IDE launch, I've watched this product evolve from a spec-driven coding tool into something approaching a genuine engineering platform. Crew is the piece that makes the others click together.

Core capabilities

Self-learning memory

This isn't just "remembers your last conversation." Crew maintains:

  • Memory: preferences, active projects, relevant history across sessions
  • Lessons: corrections you make become persistent rules. Tell it once to stop using var, and it never does again. Workspace-scoped, so project A's rules don't bleed into project B.
  • Skills: repeated patterns get synthesized into named, inspectable Markdown files.
  • Knowledge graph: architectural decisions, coding preferences, project context stored with vector embeddings and full-text search.

Everything's visible. Edit it, delete it, scope it. No magic black box learning you can't audit.

If you've been using Kiro CLI with .kiro steering files and custom skills, you already know the value of persistent instructions. Crew takes that same principle and applies it to the agent's own working memory between sessions.

Scheduled and unattended work

This is where Crew separates from every other AI coding tool I've used:

  • Cron jobs: timezone-aware, per-job timeouts, jitter to avoid thundering herds, skip dates for maintenance windows.
  • Webhooks: authenticated endpoints trigger agent work when external events arrive.
  • Heartbeats: watches state changes in PRs, deployments, pipelines. Triggers work when conditions are met.
  • Checkpoints and retries: long-running tasks save progress and resume after failures.

The key detail: jobs that don't require model reasoning run as plain scripts. No inference call, no credit consumption. A health check script costs nothing. Only reasoning costs credits.

Multi-agent orchestration

Crew can run several conversations concurrently, each with isolated context. It delegates independent research and implementation to sub-agents, then returns results to a parent conversation that stays focused on the goal.

You give it a migration task. It spawns one agent to analyze the source code, another to write the target code, another to handle tests. The parent coordinates. I've been waiting for this pattern since I started using Kiro's sub-agent feature in the CLI, which works but forces you to stay in the loop for every handoff.

Apps (purpose-built interfaces)

Some work doesn't belong in a chat window. Apps wrap agents, skills, schedules, and integrations into custom UIs:

  • DevFleets: work tree management
  • Task Runner: long-running task execution
  • Issue Radar: PR and issue triage with readiness labels
  • Code Review Sage: reviews by blast radius, stages draft GitHub reviews
  • Research Lab: fans out sub-questions to parallel agents, streams findings

Build your own with the App SDK (TypeScript or Python). Combine React UI with the agent runtime and event bus.

7 layers of security

Giving an agent real access to your code and CI demands real security. This matters especially if you're working with enterprise clients where compliance isn't optional. Crew ships with:

  1. OS-level process sandbox
  2. Tool approval gates (you decide what runs)
  3. Sensitive path blocking
  4. Write-protected paths
  5. Denied command patterns and suspicious bash blocking
  6. MCP input validation and output redaction
  7. Credential redaction and signed audit logs (SEL)

Because it's open source, you can verify every layer. Read the code, trace the execution path, confirm the sandbox actually sandboxes. For my consulting clients, the "show me the source" conversation just got a lot easier.

How it fits in the Kiro ecosystem

Kiro now has four surfaces: IDE, CLI, Web, and Crew. Here's how they relate:

Kiro IDE Kiro CLI Kiro Web Kiro Crew
Sessions Interactive Interactive Interactive Persistent, autonomous
Scheduling No No No Cron, webhooks, heartbeats
Multi-agent No Sub-agents No Full parallel orchestration
Memory Session only Session only Session only Cross-session persistent
Works unattended No No No Yes
Open source No No No Yes (Apache 2.0)

Crew runs on the Kiro CLI and reads your existing .kiro configuration. Steering files, skills, custom agents all carry over. No migration. No reconfiguration. If you already use Kiro, Crew is additive.

It also uses Agent Client Protocol (ACP) for orchestration, meaning every step is observable live. You watch how it plans, spawns sub-agents, selects tools, gates actions for approval, and synthesizes results.

Where I would have used this last month

Let me give you three real scenarios from my past few weeks where Crew would have saved me hours.

The CDK migration that stalled every evening. I was migrating a client's CloudFormation stacks to CDK. Each stack took 20-40 minutes of agent time in Kiro CLI: analyzing the template, generating CDK constructs, running cdk synth to validate. I could do maybe 3-4 stacks per session before context started degrading and I needed to re-explain the project conventions. With Crew's checkpoints and persistent memory? I could have queued all 12 stacks, let it chew through them overnight, and come back to a PR with all the synthesized outputs validated.

The Monday morning "what happened over the weekend" scramble. Every Monday I open Slack to 40+ messages, check three repos for new PRs, look at whether the weekend deploy held, and scan CloudWatch for anomalies. This takes me 45 minutes before I write a single line of code. A Crew morning digest cron job does this in 5 minutes and hands me a summary before my first coffee. Zero credits for the Slack scan and CloudWatch check (plain scripts), minimal credits for summarizing findings.

The recurring dependency update nobody does. I have a personal project with 15 npm dependencies I should update monthly. I never do. A weekly Crew heartbeat could check for security advisories, test the updates, and open a PR only when tests pass. Cost: nearly zero because most runs would be "nothing to update" (plain script check) with the occasional reasoning call when something actually needs upgrading.

These aren't hypothetical AI demos. These are the exact gaps in my current Kiro CLI workflow that made me sit up when Crew launched.

Real use cases worth trying first

Don't start with something complex. Start with work that already extends beyond one session.

Morning PR digest

Schedule a daily cron job that checks open PRs, summarizes status, and flags what needs your attention. You get a briefing before your first coffee. The plain "list open PRs" part is a script (zero credits). The "summarize what changed and whether it's ready for review" part takes one reasoning call (2-3 credits). Compare that to the 45 minutes you currently spend manually scanning GitHub every morning.

Flaky test hunter

Set a heartbeat on your CI pipeline. When a test fails twice in a row, Crew investigates the logs, identifies the pattern, and opens a fix PR. This one is personal. I have a test suite where test_concurrent_writes fails every third run due to a timing issue I've been "meaning to fix" for two months. A heartbeat that catches and fixes it without me ever opening the file? That's worth the credits.

Incident investigation across repos

Point it at an alert. It pulls logs from multiple repos, correlates timestamps, identifies the likely root cause. You stay focused on the fix while Crew handles the forensics. For anyone who's ever spent an hour jumping between CloudWatch, ECS task logs, and application traces during an incident, having a dedicated investigation agent running in parallel changes the speed of resolution.

Dependency drift detection

Weekly cron that checks for outdated packages, stale branches, docs that no longer match the code, and failing test suites nobody noticed. Most weeks it finds nothing (zero credits, plain script). When it does find something, it opens an issue with the exact versions, breaking changes, and a suggested upgrade path.

Long-running migration with checkpoints

Start a multi-hour migration. It proceeds through checkpoints, validates each step, retries failures, and you come back to progress rather than a stalled process. The CDK migration scenario I described earlier is a perfect example. Each stack is a checkpoint. If stack 7 fails validation, Crew retries with a different approach. You don't restart from stack 1.

Getting started

Prerequisites

  • Kiro account (free tier works for testing, Pro+ recommended for real use)
  • Kiro CLI installed and authenticated
  • macOS, Linux, or Windows
  • Familiarity with .kiro configuration (steering files, skills)

Installation 

# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew

# Or download from releases (macOS, Linux, Windows)
# https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew/releases

# Core commands
kirocrew chat     # Start a session
kirocrew run      # Execute a task
kirocrew cron     # Manage scheduled jobs
kirocrew spawn    # Spawn parallel agents

Your existing .kiro config carries over automatically. Steering files, skills, custom agents, all of it. If you've invested time in your Kiro setup, that investment transfers directly.

The desktop app (Electron) needs no Python or npm installation. Download and run. The web dashboard gives you multi-session chat, memory explorer, cron manager, and an app store across 14 color themes. You can also connect Slack, Telegram, Discord, or WeCom to interact with your crew from any surface.

Pricing reality check

Kiro Crew itself costs nothing. It's Apache 2.0. But agents need inference, and inference needs a Kiro plan.

Plan Monthly Cost Credits Included
Free $0 50 credits
Pro $20 1,000 credits
Pro+ $40 2,000 credits
Pro Max $100 5,000 credits
Power $200 10,000 credits

Add-on credits: $0.04 each. Scheduled jobs that run plain scripts (health checks, simple git operations) consume zero credits. Only reasoning calls cost you.

How does this compare to alternatives? Devin's Teams plan starts at $500/month (with the Core plan at $20/month for lighter usage). OpenAI Codex requires API spend that scales unpredictably. Crew's advantage: you know exactly what you're spending, and most scheduled maintenance jobs cost nothing.

The real cost question is: how many credits does a typical cron job burn? Based on my Kiro CLI usage patterns, a simple "check PRs and summarize" task runs about 2-3 credits. A complex "investigate failing tests and propose a fix" might run 8-12 credits. On the Pro plan ($20/month, 1,000 credits), you could run a morning digest every workday and still have 900+ credits for interactive work.

What to watch out for

I want to be honest about the limitations. Because every "introducing" article pretends there aren't any.

The Kiro plan dependency is real. Crew is open source, but the CLI it runs on requires a Kiro account and credits. Until someone builds and validates a connector for a different agent runtime, you're locked to Kiro's inference. Michael Leone from Moor Strategy put it directly: "Until someone runs a different agent under Crew and shows it working, the open part stops at the orchestration layer."

If you're already using Claude Code, Codex, or Devin, you can't plug them into Crew today. The ACP protocol is open, but integrations need to be built and tested. This is day one. The connectors will come, but they don't exist yet.

Parallel agents multiply costs. Three sub-agents working simultaneously burn three times the credits. I've learned this the hard way with Kiro CLI's sub-agent feature: what feels like one task can spawn four reasoning calls. Architect your workflows to use sequential execution where order matters, and parallel only for genuinely independent work.

Stephanie Walter from HyperFRAME Research raises a point I agree with from my enterprise consulting experience: before you let persistent agents operate across your repos and CI/CD pipelines, you need policies for least-privilege access, human approvals, memory retention, and auditability. The security layers exist in Crew, but your organization needs to decide how to configure them.

And the most important caveat: Crew won't architect your system. It won't make design decisions. It won't tell you whether to pick ECS over Lambda for your specific workload. It coordinates and executes. You still need to be the engineer who decides what to build and why.

The bigger picture

The trajectory is clear: AI assistants, then AI agents, now AI teams. We've been living in the "agents" phase for the past year. Kiro Crew pushes toward teams.

Not teams that replace developers. Teams that handle the integration work, the monitoring, the routine maintenance, the context reconnection between sessions. So you can spend your time on system design, architecture decisions, and the complex problems that actually need a human brain.

I think about this from an enterprise architecture perspective. Every organization I've worked with in the past three years has developers using AI coding tools in some form. But it's almost entirely shadow IT. Individual engineers wiring up their own agents, using personal credentials, nobody tracking what ran or what it touched. Michael Leone from Moor Strategy sees the same thing: "Agent use inside most companies right now is shadow IT. A shared workspace with approval gates and logging gives you one place to see what ran, what it touched, and who authorized it."

That's the real value proposition for platform engineering teams considering Crew. It's not "make developers faster." It's "make AI agent usage visible, auditable, and governable." The security layers, the signed audit logs, the approval gates, those aren't just developer niceties. They're the answer to "how do we let engineers use AI agents without losing control?"

The open-source angle matters here. A workspace with access to your code, CI, and credentials should not be a black box. You should read the source, trace the execution, verify the security layers. Kiro Crew ships that transparency on day one. For anyone who's been burned by opaque AI tools that silently send your code to third-party servers, this matters.

Whether you adopt it today or wait for the ecosystem to mature, this pattern is the direction. Persistent, self-learning, multi-agent workspaces that work alongside you across sessions. The question isn't whether this becomes standard. It's who builds theirs first.

Michael Leone from Moor Strategy sees the same thing: "Agent use inside most companies right now is shadow IT. A shared workspace with approval gates and logging gives you one place to see what ran, what it touched, and who authorized it." That's the real value proposition for platform engineering teams considering Crew. It's not "make developers faster." It's "make AI agent usage visible, auditable, and governable." The security layers, the signed audit logs, the approval gates, those aren't just developer niceties. They're the answer to "how do we let engineers use AI agents without losing control?" The open-source angle matters here. A workspace with access to your code, CI, and credentials should not be a black box. You should read the source, trace the execution, verify the security layers. Kiro Crew ships that transparency on day one. For anyone who's been burned by opaque AI tools that silently send your code to third-party servers, this matters. Whether you adopt it today or wait for the ecosystem to mature, this pattern is the direction. Persistent, self-learning, multi-agent workspaces that work alongside you across sessions. Kiro Crew 到底是什么

Kiro Crew 是一个开源 (Apache 2.0) 的持久开发工作区。 一个编排层，可协调多个 AI 代理、保留跨会话的上下文、安排重复工作并在离线时保持运行。

起源故事很重要。 亚马逊内部的三名工程师开发了一个名为 MeshClaw 的业余项目。 他们想要一些简单的事情：开始一项任务，走开，回来做一些可审查的事情。 一次运行多项任务，而不是一次处理一个提示。

然后其他亚马逊建设者接手了它。 不是因为有人强制这样做。 因为工程师不断地发现工作流程中的漏洞、修复它们，并将修复推向上游。 在不到六个月的时间里，超过 39,000 名亚马逊开发者采用了它。 近 500 名贡献者以平均每周 143 次提交的速度发布了 597 项更新。

有机采用是最强烈的信号。 数千名工程师选择使用它，数百名工程师选择改进它，这一事实比任何功能列表都更能告诉您。

它解决的问题（以及我为什么关心）

在跨客户参与构建云基础设施十多年之后，我接受了一个令人沮丧的事实：我花更多的时间作为工具之间的“粘合剂”，而不是做实际的工程工作。

Kiro Crew 博客文章指出了这一点。 开发人员是他们自己的工具之间的集成层。

我每天都有这样的感觉。 我打开了 Kiro CLI，在一个选项卡中打开了 CloudWatch，在另一个选项卡中打开了 GitHub，我需要跟进一个 Slack 线程，三个 PR 等待审核，以及一个一夜之间崩溃的部署。 当我离开的那一刻，一切都停止了。 没有人重新连接上下文。 没有人推动迁移前进。 没有人注意到不稳定的测试再次出现。

我已经使用 Kiro CLI 几个月了。 在单个会话中效果很好。 你提示，它回应，它确实工作得很好。 但关闭选项卡？ 下次您打开它时，上下文就会消失。 你用前十分钟重新解释你正在做的事情。 您的转向文件会保留，但“我们在哪里？”的工作记忆会保留。 没有。

Kiro Crew 通过使工作空间持久化来打破这种模式。 记忆继续前进。 纠正成为持久的教训。 重复的模式成为可重复使用的技能。 即使您不在键盘前，工作也能按计划继续进行。

作为一名自 IDE 发布以来一直在撰写有关 Kiro 的 AWS 社区构建者，我见证了该产品从规范驱动的编码工具发展成为接近真正的工程平台的东西。 《Crew》是让其他人齐心协力的作品。

核心能力

自学记忆

这不仅仅是“记住你上次的谈话”。 船员坚持：

  • 记忆：偏好、活动项目、跨会话的相关历史记录
  • 教训：你所做的更正将成为持久的规则。 一旦告诉它停止使用 var，它就再也不会这样做了。 工作空间范围内，因此项目 A 的规则不会渗透到项目 B 中。
  • 技能：重复的模式被合成到命名的、可检查的 Markdown 文件中。
  • 知识图：架构决策、编码偏好、使用向量嵌入存储的项目上下文和全文搜索。

一切都可见。 编辑它、删除它、确定范围。 没有无法审核的神奇黑匣子学习。

如果您一直在使用带有 .kiro 引导文件和自定义技能的 Kiro CLI，那么您已经知道持久指令的价值。 Crew 采用了同样的原则，并将其应用到代理在会话之间的工作记忆中。

预定和无人值守的工作

这就是 Crew 与我使用过的所有其他人工智能编码工具的不同之处：

  • Cron 作业：时区感知、每个作业超时、抖动以避免惊群、跳过维护窗口的日期。
  • Webhooks：当外部事件到达时，经过身份验证的端点会触发代理工作。
  • 心跳：监视 PR、部署、管道中的状态变化。 触发器在满足条件时起作用。
  • 检查点和重试：长时间运行的任务保存进度并在失败后恢复。

关键细节：不需要模型推理的作业作为普通脚本运行。 没有推理调用，没有信用消费。 健康检查脚本不需要任何费用。 只有推理才需要学分。

多代理编排

Crew 可以同时运行多个对话，每个对话都有独立的上下文。 它将独立研究和实施委托给子代理，然后将结果返回给专注于目标的父级对话。

您给它一个迁移任务。 它生成一个代理来分析源代码，另一个代理来编写目标代码，另一个代理来处理测试。 父坐标。 自从我开始在 CLI 中使用 Kiro 的子代理功能以来，我一直在等待这种模式，它可以工作，但会迫使您在每次切换时都处于循环状态。

应用程序（专用界面）

有些工作不属于聊天窗口。 应用程序将代理、技能、计划和集成包装到自定义 UI 中：

  • DevFleets：工作树管理
  • Task Runner：长时间运行的任务执行
  • 问题雷达：公关和带有就绪标签的问题分类
  • Code Review Sage：按爆炸半径进行评论，阶段草稿 GitHub 评论
  • 研究实验室：将子问题分散给并行代理，流式传输结果

使用 App SDK（TypeScript 或 Python）构建您自己的应用程序。 将 React UI 与代理运行时和事件总线结合起来。

7层安全保障

让代理真正访问您的代码和 CI 需要真正的安全性。 如果您与企业客户合作，而合规性是不可选择的，这一点尤其重要。 船员随船携带：

  1. 操作系统级进程沙箱
  2. 工具批准门（您决定运行什么）
  3. 敏感路径阻塞
  4. 写保护路径
  5. 拒绝命令模式和可疑的 bash 阻止
  6. MCP 输入验证和输出编辑
  7. 凭证编辑和签名审核日志 (SEL)

因为它是开源的，所以您可以验证每一层。 阅读代码，跟踪执行路径，确认沙箱确实是沙箱。 对于我的咨询客户来说，“向我展示来源”对话变得更加容易。

Kiro 现在有四个界面：IDE、CLI、Web 和 Crew。 以下是它们的关系：

让我给你展示过去几周的三个真实场景，在这些场景中，Crew 可以节省我的时间。

CDK 迁移每天晚上都停滞不前。 我正在将客户的 CloudFormation 堆栈迁移到 CDK。 每个堆栈在 Kiro CLI 中花费了 20-40 分钟的代理时间：分析模板、生成 CDK 构造、运行 cdk 合成器进行验证。 在上下文开始退化之前，我每个会话可能会执行 3-4 个堆栈，并且我需要重新解释项目约定。 有了船员的检查点和持久记忆？ 我可以对所有 12 个堆栈进行排队，让它在一夜之间仔细研究它们，然后返回 PR，并验证所有合成输出。

周一早上“周末发生的事情”争先恐后。 每个星期一我都会打开 Slack 并收到 40 多条消息，检查三个存储库中是否有新的 PR，查看周末部署是否成功，并扫描 CloudWatch 是否存在异常情况。 我花了 45 分钟才写出一行代码。 Crew 的早晨摘要 cron 作业只需​​ 5 分钟即可完成此操作，并在我喝第一杯咖啡之前递给我一份摘要。 Slack 扫描和 CloudWatch 检查（纯脚本）零积分，总结结果的最低积分。

没有人会重复进行依赖更新。 我有一个个人项目，有 15 个 npm 依赖项，我应该每月更新一次。 我从来不这样做。 每周一次的 Crew 心跳可以检查安全建议、测试更新，并仅在测试通过时打开 PR。 成本：几乎为零，因为大多数运行都是“没有什么可更新的”（简单的脚本检查），当某些东西确实需要升级时，偶尔会进行推理调用。

这些不是假设的人工智能演示。 这些正是我当前的 Kiro CLI 工作流程中的缺陷，当 Crew 推出时，这些缺陷让我坐立不安。

值得首先尝试的真实用例

不要从复杂的事情开始。 从已经超出一次会议范围的工作开始。

早间公关摘要

安排每日 cron 作业来检查开放的 PR、总结状态并标记需要您注意的内容。 在喝第一杯咖啡之前，您会收到简报。 简单的“列出开放 PR”部分是一个脚本（零学分）。 “总结发生了什么变化以及是否准备好进行审查”部分需要一次推理调用（2-3 学分）。 与此相比，您目前每天早上手动扫描 GitHub 的时间为 45 分钟。

不稳定的测试猎人

在 CI 管道上设置心跳。 当测试连续两次失败时，Crew 会调查日志、识别模式并打开修复 PR。 这是个人的。 我有一个测试套件，其中 test_concurrent_writes 每三次运行都会失败，因为我两个月来一直“打算修复”计时问题。 无需我打开文件就能捕获并修复它的心跳？ 这是值得的。

跨仓库的事件调查

将其指向警报。 它从多个存储库中提取日志，关联时间戳，识别可能的根本原因。 您可以专注于修复，而 Crew 则负责取证。 对于在事件期间花费一个小时在 CloudWatch、ECS 任务日志和应用程序跟踪之间切换的任何人来说，并行运行专用调查代理会改变解决速度。

依赖性漂移检测

每周 cron 检查过时的软件包、过时的分支、不再与代码匹配的文档以及无人注意到的失败测试套件。 大多数星期它什么也没发现（零学分，简单的脚本）。 当它确实找到某些内容时，它会提出一个问题，其中包含确切的版本、重大更改和建议的升级路径。

带有检查点的长时间运行的迁移

开始一个多小时的迁移。 它会通过检查点，验证每个步骤，重试失败，然后您就会恢复正常，而不是陷入停滞的过程。 我之前描述的 CDK 迁移场景就是一个完美的例子。 每个堆栈都是一个检查点。 如果堆栈 7 验证失败，Crew 将使用不同的方法重试。 您不会从堆栈 1 重新启动。

需要注意什么

我想诚实地了解这些限制。 因为每一篇“介绍”文章都假装没有。

Kiro 计划的依赖性是真实存在的。 Crew 是开源的，但它运行的 CLI 需要 Kiro 帐户和积分。 在有人为不同的代理运行时构建并验证连接器之前，您将被锁定到 Kiro 的推理中。 Moor Strategy 的 Michael Leone 直接指出：“除非有人在 Crew 的领导下运行不同的代理并展示其工作原理，否则开放部分将停留在编排层。”

如果您已经在使用 Claude Code、Codex 或 Devin，那么您现在无法将它们插入 Crew。 ACP 协议是开放的，但需要构建和测试集成。 这是第一天。 连接器将会出现，但它们还不存在。

并行代理会成倍增加成本。 三个子代理同时工作会消耗三倍的积分。 我通过 Kiro CLI 的子代理功能艰难地了解到了这一点：感觉一个任务可以产生四个推理调用。 构建您的工作流程，以便在顺序很重要的情况下使用顺序执行，并且仅在真正独立的工作中使用并行执行。

来自 HyperFRAME Research 的 Stephanie Walter 提出了我在企业咨询经验中同意的一个观点：在让持久代理在您的存储库和 CI/CD 管道中运行之前，您需要最低权限访问、人工批准、内存保留和可审计性的策略。 Crew 中存在安全层，但您的组织需要决定如何配置它们。

最重要的警告：Crew 不会构建您的系统。 它不会做出设计决策。 它不会告诉您是否针对特定工作负载选择 ECS 而不是 Lambda。 它协调并执行。 您仍然需要成为决定构建什么以及为什么构建的工程师。

更大的图景

发展轨迹很明确：人工智能助理，然后是人工智能代理，现在是人工智能团队。 过去一年我们一直生活在“代理”阶段。 Kiro Crew 向团队推进。

不是取代开发人员的团队。 处理集成工作、监控、日常维护、会话之间的上下文重新连接的团队。 因此，您可以将时间花在系统设计、架构决策以及真正需要人脑参与的复杂问题上。

我从企业架构的角度来思考这个问题。 过去三年里我合作过的每个组织都有开发人员以某种形式使用人工智能编码工具。 但它几乎完全是影子IT。 个别工程师使用个人凭证连接自己的代理，没有人跟踪运行的内容或接触的内容。 Moor Strategy 的 Michael Leone 也有同样的看法：“目前大多数公司内部使用的代理都是影子 IT。 具有批准门和日志记录的共享工作区让您可以在一个地方查看运行的内容、触及的内容以及授权者。”

对于考虑 Crew 的平台工程团队来说，这才是真正的价值主张。 它不是“让开发人员更快”。 它“让人工智能代理的使用可见、可审计、可管理”。 安全层、签名的审核日志、审批门，这些不仅仅是开发人员的细节。 它们是“我们如何让工程师在不失去控制的情况下使用人工智能代理？”的答案。

开源角度在这里很重要。 可以访问代码、CI 和凭据的工作区不应该是黑匣子。 您应该阅读源代码，跟踪执行情况，验证安全层。 Kiro Crew 在第一天就实现了透明度。 对于那些被不透明的人工智能工具所困扰的人来说，这些工具会悄悄地将代码发送到第三方服务器，这很重要。

无论你今天采用还是等待生态系统成熟，这种模式都是方向。 持续、自学习、多代理工作空​​间，可跨会话与您一起工作。 问题不在于这是否会成为标准。 谁先建造他们的。
